ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is red‑cell destruction by autoantibodies, causing anaemia and jaundice. Diagnosis hinges on a positive direct antiglobulin test and clinical clues. Management starts with treating the underlying cause and immunosuppression.

sections.p: AIHA is immune‑mediated red‑cell lysis, usually by IgG (warm) or IgM (cold) antibodies. The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is the diagnostic cornerstone, showing antibody or complement coating the cell surface.
b: DAT negative = consider other haemolysis causes

t.b: Detects IgG or complement on RBCs; positive confirms immune haemolysis.
Shows spherocytes or schistocytes; spherocytes suggest warm AIHA.
Elevated indicates marrow response to haemolysis.
High LDH, indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin confirm haemolysis.

sections.p: Severity is graded by haemoglobin level, bilirubin, and need for transfusion. WHO anaemia grades (mild, moderate, severe) guide urgency of treatment.
b: Hb <7 g/dL or transfusion need = severe

t.b: Measures anaemia severity; guides transfusion threshold.
High indirect bilirubin indicates ongoing haemolysis.

sections.p: Primary AIHA is idiopathic. Secondary causes are common in low‑resource settings: infections (malaria, HIV, TB), autoimmune diseases (SLE), malignancies (CLL), drugs, and herbal remedies.
Patients report fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine, and sometimes splenomegaly. Warm AIHA often presents with sudden drop in Hb and haemoglobinuria.
b: Rapid Hb fall in cold AIHA

sections.p: Confirm haemolysis and rule out other causes. When tests are unavailable, clinical judgement and basic labs guide management.
b: Bone marrow if haemoglobin <7 g/dL and unclear cause

sections.p: Severe haemolysis can lead to hypovolaemic shock, renal failure, and hyperbilirubinaemic jaundice. Rapid drop in Hb or rising bilirubin warrants urgent care.
b: Signs of DIC in severe cases

sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger first. Immunosuppression with steroids is first line; alternatives include rituximab or splenectomy if refractory. Supportive care includes transfusion and monitoring.
b: Avoid transfusing incompatible blood; use washed RBCs if severe alloimmunisation

sections.p: Monitor Hb, bilirubin, and reticulocytes. Educate patients on avoiding triggers, such as certain drugs and herbal remedies. Vaccinate against infections that can precipitate AIHA.
Hemolytic transfusion reactions, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, and malaria can mimic AIHA.
DAT can be negative in early or mixed AIHA; low haptoglobin may be falsely normal in liver disease. Low reticulocyte count may mask severe haemolysis if marrow is suppressed.
b: Reticulocyte count low in aplastic crisis

faq.q: What is the most common type of AIHA?
faq.a: Warm AIHA, mediated by IgG antibodies reacting at body temperature.
No, AIHA is acquired; hereditary haemolytic anaemias are separate conditions.

faq.q: Is a blood transfusion safe in AIHA?
faq.a: Yes, but use washed or antigen‑matched blood and monitor for reactions.
